Sample.evidence_source: Informants were 30 patients (12 men and 18 women) between 18 and 46 years of age admitted to hospital following a suicide attempt (by means of self-poisoning with various substances).

Country.evidence_source: Data were collected at five hospitals and clinics in Accra. Informants were mostly Christian with only two being Muslim. They were asked to describe what led to the suicide attempt, the act itself and the reaction of those around them. Though a direct question was asked in the course of the interview on how religion featured in their experiences, for most informants, religious reflections and experiences had spontaneously emerged while describing the suicidal experience. The interviews took place within a week of the act and were narrative in nature, a process that allowed informants to refer to the actual concrete events in space and time, suffusing these experiences with meaning and significance. Here, we present emerging themes relating to how informants perceived and understood their suicidal experiences in a religious context. All interviews were conducted by the first author who is a native Ghanaian psychologist.
